story: Ghana's gold is literally poisoning its water. Illegal miners, known as galamsey, have turned rivers like the Pra and Ankobra the colour of milky tea, killing fish, ruining cocoa farms and forcing water utilities to shut treatment plants. President John Mahama won back the presidency in late 2024 promising to stop it. Two years in, it remains the weakest part of his record, and critics say the reason is simple: gold exports are keeping the economy afloat after Ghana's 2022 default, so no government wants to choke them off (KAS, Citi Newsroom).

Everything else looked like recovery. In his 2026 State of the Nation address, Mahama said the economy was "in take-off mode" and signed the law creating his 24-Hour Economy Authority on 19 February, his plan to create jobs by keeping factories, ports and services running around the clock for a country where young people struggle most to find work (GBC). Abroad, Ghana pushed a UN resolution declaring the transatlantic slave trade a crime against humanity, a claim with real weight from a country whose coastal forts held enslaved people before the crossing. Ghana remains West Africa's steadiest democracy, with power changing hands peacefully at the ballot box, which makes the galamsey failure more pointed: it is a problem voters chose Mahama to fix.
briefing.power: A presidential republic. The president is directly elected for four years with a two-term limit and heads the government; the 276-seat Parliament is elected by first-past-the-post. Two parties, Mahama's NDC and the NPP, have alternated in power since 1992.
briefing.holders: President John Dramani Mahama (NDC), in office since January 2025.
